questions.prompt: The modern Internet has its origins in ARPANET, a research network developed in the late 1960s in the United States.
questions.explanation: ARPANET, US, late 1960s. The Internet's predecessor was funded by the US Department of Defense's ARPA and connected research universities; commercial growth followed once NSFNET was retired in the 1990s. Layering & Architecture

questions.prompt: Layered architectures separate responsibilities across the protocol stack. Which of the following is a key benefit that layering gives the Internet?

choices.A: It lets different technologies and protocols evolve independently, as long as each layer keeps the same interface to the layer above.
choices.B: It guarantees that every packet is delivered in the original order it was sent, with no possibility of loss along the path.
choices.C: It removes the need for any headers in the data units that are transmitted between hosts on the Internet.
choices.D: It eliminates the need for routers at the network layer entirely, even in very large interconnected networks.

questions.explanation: Stable interfaces => layers evolve independently. As long as each layer keeps its contract with the layer above, the implementation below can change (e.g., Ethernet -> fiber -> Wi-Fi) without rewriting higher layers.

questions.prompt: Encapsulation works as follows: when data moves down the stack at the sender, each layer adds its own header. When data moves up at the receiver, each layer removes the header added by the corresponding layer at the sender.
questions.explanation: Sender adds headers going down; receiver strips them going up. Each layer wraps its peer's view with its own header on transmit, and the receiver's matching layer removes that header before passing the payload upward.
questions.figureCaption: Figure: Layered encapsulation across the protocol stack (Module 1)

questions.prompt: An IP address alone is sufficient to deliver an incoming packet to the correct application process on a host, without using port numbers.
questions.explanation: IP gets you to the host, not the process. Without port numbers in the transport header, the OS can't decide whether a packet belongs to your browser, your SSH client, or your mail daemon - all of them share the same IP. Connection Oriented and Connectionless Multiplexing and Demultiplexing

questions.prompt: In the figure, two hosts initiate HTTP sessions to the same web server B on port 80. If both clients happen to pick the same source port number, how does server B still keep the connections separate?

choices.A: It refuses one of the two connections because source ports must always be globally unique across the public Internet for every concurrent TCP flow worldwide.
choices.B: It demultiplexes by inspecting the URL inside the application-layer payload of the GET request - the URL is what truly identifies a unique HTTP session.
choices.C: It assigns each client a freshly-allocated destination port at handshake time, signalled with a TCP option attached to the SYNACK so that two clients never share a destination port.
choices.D: It uses source IP (part of the 4-tuple) to distinguish the two sockets.

questions.explanation: Source IP breaks the tie. If two clients happen to choose the same source port, the 4-tuple still differs in the source-IP component - so the server's TCP can distinguish the two connections.
questions.figureCaption: Figure: Multiple HTTP sessions to one web server (Module 2)

questions.prompt: In the link-state example figure, source u has direct neighbors v, x, w. After initialization, x is added to N' first in iteration 1. Why x and not v or w?

choices.A: Because x has the lowest initial D value among the nodes not yet in N'.
choices.B: Because x is alphabetically last among the three candidate neighbors.
choices.C: Because x has the largest fan-out (most neighbors outside N') and Dijkstra prioritizes high-degree nodes early in convergence.
choices.D: Because v and w are not direct neighbors of u; only x is connected at all in the initialization stage.

questions.explanation: Lowest-D candidate is added next. Dijkstra's greedy choice: pick the unsettled node with smallest current D, because (with non-negative weights) no shorter path to it can exist via any other unsettled node.

questions.prompt: This figure depicts the Internet topology shifting from strictly hierarchical to flatter. What development drove most of this flattening?

choices.A: The Internet now has fewer total ASes than it had a decade ago.
choices.B: Tier-1 ISPs absorbed all Tier-2 networks via mergers, removing the middle tier.
choices.C: Large content providers and CDNs deployed at IXPs let networks bypass higher tiers for popular content.
choices.D: BGP was redesigned to forbid customer-provider relationships and require flat peering.

questions.explanation: CDNs/content providers colocate at IXPs => bypass higher tiers. Popular content (Netflix, YouTube, Akamai) lives close to eyeballs at IXPs, so traffic no longer needs to climb the hierarchy through Tier-1 transit links. AS Business Relationships
questions.figureCaption: Figure: Flattening of the Internet topology (Module 4)

questions.prompt: In a modern router, the data plane operates at nanosecond timescales in hardware, while the control plane operates at second/millisecond timescales in software.
questions.explanation: Data plane = ns (HW); control plane = ms-to-s (SW). Per-packet decisions must complete in nanoseconds to sustain line rate; routing protocols and FIB recomputation have orders of magnitude more headroom. Different Types of Switching

questions.prompt: From the HOL-blocking figure, what is head-of-line blocking in an input-queued switch?

choices.A: Packets get reordered as they cross the switching fabric during congestion, reflecting how the routing decision flows through a typical commercial-grade daemon at scale.
choices.B: An output queue drops packets when its buffer overflows during a microburst.
choices.C: The control plane stalls while waiting for a forwarding-table update at the input port.
choices.D: A packet at the front of an input queue blocks packets behind it that could otherwise be forwarded to currently-free outputs.

questions.explanation: HOL blocking: head packet pins the queue. When the first packet in an input queue can't be served (its output is busy), packets behind it cannot advance even if their outputs are idle - the input is structurally blocked.
questions.figureCaption: Figure: Head-of-line blocking pattern over packet-times - take-a-ticket (Module 6)

questions.prompt: The lesson presents SDN by contrasting it with conventional networks built from proprietary middleboxes. Which of the following are genuine advantages of the SDN approach as described in the lesson?

choices.A: A common control platform can express firewall, NAT, and load-balancing policies as applications, instead of a separate proprietary middlebox for each function.
choices.B: Deploying SDN removes the need for firewalls, NAT, and load balancers.
choices.C: Every network application works from the same global view of the network, keeping policy decisions consistent and letting control-plane modules be reused.
choices.D: A network function's logic can run from anywhere in the network, rather than being pinned to a fixed physical location the way middleboxes were.
choices.E: Each switch hosts its own copy of the controller and recomputes the global forwarding policy on its own.
choices.F: Independent applications, such as routing and load balancing, can be combined and integrated more smoothly.
choices.G: The control and data planes stay bundled inside each device, now running on faster hardware.
choices.H: Decoupling the control plane from the data plane lets new features and protocols roll out without upgrading firmware on every device.

questions.explanation: A / C / D / F are the four advantages the "SDN Advantages" page names — shared abstractions, consistent global network view, location-independent placement, and simpler integration. H is the core motivation benefit: decoupling the planes ends the per-device, ~10-year rollout cycle. B is the classic trap — those functions aren't removed; they become applications on the controller. E is wrong — control is logically centralized (a controller, physically distributed in practice), not replicated per switch. G is wrong — SDN's whole premise is decoupling the control and data planes, not keeping them bundled.
